items.title: Iran may be working on biological weapons, Trump says
items.summary: President Trump told Fox News there are indications Iran may be working on biological or chemical weapons as the war drags on toward its ninth month.
items.t: Iran ramps up retaliation on Gulf countries after U.S. strikes

items.title: Ukraine’s allies meet in Berlin with air defence, energy and financial support on the agenda – Europe live
items.summary:
Meeting comes after Trump declared Putin a ‘friend’ during trilateral meeting in China

For what it’s worth, the China-US-Russia ‘peace declaration’ issued after their meeting, and published by Chinese state media, includes absolutely no mention of Ukraine or Europe whatsoever.

There is only one, rather generic, line that could be seen as close to these issues:

“The three heads of state exchanged in-depth views on the current international situation and pledged to maintain strategic stability and international security.”

Continue reading...
items.t: Tusk appears to mock Trump’s Putin comment as Ukraine’s allies meet in Berlin – Europe live

items.title: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
items.summary:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’

  • Apec summit – latest updates

China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

Continue reading...
items.t: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

items.title: ‘New page in history?’ Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote
items.summary:
Far from the grand ambitions declared in Yalta in 1945, Shenzhen felt like a meeting in search of an agenda

  • Apec summit – latest updates

It is arguably true, given it was the first such meeting of the leaders of China, Russia and the US, that Thursday’s gathering in Shenzhen deserved the description of “historic”.

But in terms of tangible outcomes, it is unlikely to warrant the “new page in the history of diplomacy” that Vladimir Putin claimed had been written, and will instead be consigned to a smallish footnote in any future volume of the 21st century.

Continue reading...
items.t: ‘New page in history?’ Xi, Trump and Putin summit was more of a footnote

items.title: Gender pay gap: French women work "for free” from today
items.summary: Women in Europe are still paid less than men, with the gap falling from 15.1% in 2016 to 11.1% in 2024, according to Eurostat. In France, women symbolically start working for free from 10:51 am on Thursday, 19 November, and at the current pace equality would not be reached until 2062. Experts warn that AI could make things worse by eliminating administrative and legal jobs where many women work, while childbirth and short paternity leave continue to slow women’s careers.
items.t: Gender pay gap: French women work "for free” from today

items.title: 'GTA VI': A masterpiece? Fans react to gaming's biggest release
items.summary: Critics are calling the new "Grand Theft Auto VI" a masterpiece. In this edition of arts24, we hear what fans make of one of the biggest video game releases in history. We also look at U2's new album and tour marking 50 years of the band, discover the French comic book that Pope Leo is reading and meet the women redefining Mexico's Mariachi tradition.
items.t: 'GTA VI': A masterpiece? Fans react to gaming's biggest release

items.title: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches
items.summary:
Andy Burnham due in Brussels on Friday but sticking points on food rules and tuition fees remain unresolved

The UK-EU reset talks will go “down to the wire” as the British government battles to have a say in shaping future European food and farming rules.

With less than 24 hours to go before Andy Burnham is due in Brussels for a summit with EU leaders, the two sides still need to resolve some central sticking points, including how much of a say Britain will have in new EU food rules.

Continue reading...
items.t: UK-EU reset talks will go ‘down to the wire’ as crunch summit approaches

items.title: The chocolate countdown: The art of the advent calendar
items.summary: The holiday season is almost upon us and with it come advent calendars. The annual physical countdown originated in 19th-century Germany as a Christian tradition to count down the days until Christmas. Eugénie Pont from the magazine Fou de Pâtisserie tells us more about what we can expect from the biggest chocolate makers in France.
items.t: The chocolate countdown: The art of the advent calendar

items.title: Trump, Xi, Putin summit: What was it all about?
items.summary: Donald Trump has left China after a historic first meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit. Ukraine was discussed without Kyiv or European leaders in the room, which raised eyebrows, though Trump defended dialogue with rivals and Putin said the talks created conditions for future agreements. Xi warned major powers against conflict, and topics included reducing nuclear risks, reforming the UN and increasing energy flows.
items.t: Trump, Xi, Putin summit: What was it all about?

items.title: Behind the UK's use of AI in asylum applications
items.summary: The UK is increasingly turning to artificial intelligence to manage its immigration system, from analysing migrants’ phones to processing asylum applications. But what happens when AI gets involved in deciding how an asylum seeker's story is understood? Stella Elgersma, journalist at InfoMigrants, explains how the UK Home Office is testing AI tools to process asylum applications, including a system that generates summaries of asylum interviews. With errors, limited human oversight and concerns over transparency, could AI put asylum seekers’ lives at risk?
items.t: Behind the UK's use of AI in asylum applications

items.title: Haiti: Salvador’s Bukele publishes video of attack on gang leader’s house
items.summary: Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele said Wednesday that his troops demolished the lavish home of a prominent gang leader in Haiti known as Jeff Gwo Lwa. "My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières," Bukele wrote on X - referencing a 1803 battle critical in helping secure Haiti's independence from France.
items.t: Haiti: Salvador’s Bukele publishes video of attack on gang leader’s house

items.title: EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack using AI tools
items.summary: The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.
items.t: EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack using AI tools

items.title: Beaujolais Nouveau: A French tradition uncorked
items.summary: Every year on the third Thursday of November, France raises a glass to one of its most joyful traditions: Le Beaujolais Nouveau! That means that this Thursday, millions of bottles of the 2026 young red wine will be uncorked around the world, from Lyon to New York. Olivier Badoureaux, wine expert and director of the French trade organisation Inter Beaujolais, tells us what we should expect from this year's vintage.
items.t: Beaujolais Nouveau: A French tradition uncorked

items.title: Trump, Xi and Putin sit down for a rare 3-way meeting in China
items.summary: Russia says Putin, Trump and China's Xi agreed during a rare meeting to boost gas and oil production, and "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war."
items.t: Trump and Xi speak at APEC summit ahead of rare joint meeting with Putin

items.title: France: Retirees march against 2027 budget cuts
items.summary: More than a thousand people marched in Paris on Thursday, called by a union alliance joined by student and high-school groups, to protest social and tax measures targeting retirees in the 2027 budgets. The government wants retirees to contribute about €5.4 billion, by freezing the indexation of pensions above €1,260 and reforming their 10% income tax allowance. Union leaders say the money should not come from retirees’ pockets, as FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago explains.
items.t: France: Retirees march against 2027 budget cuts

items.t: 🔴 AI firm Anthropic begins trading on Nasdaq, aiming to raise $81 billion in biggest IPO on record

items.title: Chef Rachel Khoo: 'You don't need fancy kitchen gadgets to cook delicious food'
items.summary: One of the world's best-known chefs has spoken to FRANCE 24 about her new book that proves you certainly don't need fancy kitchen gadgets to cook delicious meals. The book "The Smallest Restaurant in Paris" tells her own story of starting out in a tiny Parisian flat cooking food just for two people at a time. That then led to a BBC series and a decade of writing and filming cooking stories. Rachel Khoo is now a judge on "The Great Australian Bake Off". She spoke to us in Perspective.
items.t: Chef Rachel Khoo: 'You don't need fancy kitchen gadgets to cook delicious food'

items.title: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
items.summary: In August 2017, after attacks by a Rohingya militia, Myanmar’s army launched a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state, with survivors describing mass killings, rapes and burned villages as hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh. The Gambia took Myanmar to the ICJ in 2019, and after a seven-year legal fight the court has ruled that Myanmar committed acts of genocide. Meanwhile some 1.2 million Rohingya remain in crowded camps, unable to return home.
items.t: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya

items.title: China summit ends with little new, Europe backs Ukraine in Berlin
items.summary: The leaders of China, the United States and Russia met in Shenzhen for a historic first, but the summit brought little new: non-binding statements on peace and no plan to meet regularly. In Berlin, Europeans gathered to show their support for Ukraine, a pointed answer to a summit where Europe had no seat, as FRANCE 24's Kethevane Gorjestani explains.
items.t: China summit ends with little new, Europe backs Ukraine in Berlin

items.title: Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping
items.summary:
Reported proposal to give musicians special treatment is ‘unworkable’, Aria CEO says, vowing to stand with other creatives

  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The music industry will not accept an AI carveout deal that leaves other creative sectors behind, rejecting a reported proposal to give musicians special treatment while allowing big tech to train on other copyrighted material – described by David Pocock as a “divide and conquer strategy”.

The trade union representing writers and creatives is “alarmed” at a proposal to let AI companies train on Australian data if they buy a permit, an idea also strongly rebuffed by the Coalition and Greens.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Continue reading...
items.t: Australian music industry rejects ‘divide and conquer’ proposal to give musicians exemption from AI scraping

items.title: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message
items.summary:
Australian physicists chose to transmit the word ‘gravity’ in binary code through brick wall

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian scientists have used gravity as a means of communication, in a proof-of-concept experiment involving a snail-paced 1950s elevator, a brick wall and a men’s bathroom.

Physicists at the University of Queensland have used gravity to transmit a “practically unblockable” message about 70cm through a brick wall, by sending an elevator up and down between two floors and measuring changes in the gravitational field as a result of the movement.

Continue reading...
items.t: An elevator, a brick wall and a bathroom: scientists use gravity to send ‘practically unblockable’ message

items.t: Pakistan minister to visit India, but no breakthrough expected

items.title: In South Korea, women forced into prostitution on US military bases seek justice
items.summary: Tens of thousands of women were forced to work in South Korean state-sanctioned brothels used by American soldiers based in the country after the Korean War. They were raped, physically abused and forcibly confined. Now, after decades of silence, some of these women are speaking out.
items.t: In South Korea, women forced into prostitution on US military bases seek justice

items.title: 'Their lives, their rights, their history': Not the end of accountability for the Rohingya people'
items.summary: Oliver Farry welcomes Sonya Sceats, Director and CEO of the British Institute of International and Comparative Law. The case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar before the ICJ, and the court ruling, both have great significance for the Rohingya people, the interpretation of the Genocide Convention and the possibility of future criminal proceedings. The case could also have important implications for South Africa's proceedings against Israel, where there are “many similarities between the two cases.”
items.t: 'Their lives, their rights, their history': Not the end of accountability for the Rohingya people'

items.title: What to know about Xi, Putin and Trump's historic trilateral summit
items.summary: China's Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump met for a historic summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday, where they agreed on a "peace declaration". The three leaders pledged to reform the UN, increase supplies of refined petroleum products and uphold the immunity enjoyed by officials in international courts.
items.t: What to know about Xi, Putin and Trump's historic trilateral summit

items.title: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?
items.summary:
Leaders will wrestle with easing Brexit red tape, restoring emissions trading and opening up youth mobility

  • UK politics live – latest updates

The EU and UK will hold a long-awaited summit in Brussels on Friday – the second since Brexit – to hammer out the UK’s longer-term relationship with the bloc.

It will be attended by the prime minister, Andy Burnham, the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.

items.t: What is at stake at the EU-UK summit in Brussels?

items.title: Danish MPs approve Greenland security pact with US
items.summary:
Danish foreign minister says deal ‘removes all uncertainty’ over territory but warns trust in US needs rebuilding

  • Europe live – latest updates

The Danish parliament has unanimously approved a new Arctic security pact between Greenland, Denmark and the US in what it is hoped will mark a new chapter in relations, months after Donald Trump’s threats to invade the largely autonomous territory.

The deal, which was signed by the US president and the prime ministers of Greenland and Denmark, Jens-Frederik Nielsen and Mette Frederiksen, in September after months of talks, updates a 1951 defence agreement to give the US underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system.

Continue reading...

items.title: Nigeria: States set to get their own police forces
items.summary: Nigeria has moved a step closer to letting its 36 states set up their own police forces. The National Assembly has sent a constitutional amendment bill to the president, as authorities seek state-run police to complement the federal force amid growing insecurity. Many states currently fund vigilante groups to fight armed groups like Boko Haram, but these groups are poorly trained and ill-equipped for the task. FRANCE 24's correspondent has the latest.
items.t: Nigeria: States set to get their own police forces

items.title: French 2027 presidential race: Green leader Tondelier draws closer to hard-left Mélenchon
items.summary: Six months before the first round of France’s presidential election, Green party leader Marine Tondelier is moving closer to Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the radical left. The move has caught the other candidates on the left and in the centre off guard, notably Raphaël Glucksmann. FRANCE 24's Clovis Casali explains.
items.t: French 2027 presidential race: Green leader Tondelier draws closer to hard-left Mélenchon

items.title: Senegal: Pastef removes President Faye from its ranks
items.summary: In Senegal, Pastef, the majority party led by National Assembly president Ousmane Sonko, has made official the departure of President Bassirou Diomaye Faye. It is the latest episode in a split with his former Prime minister that was already largely complete, and it comes in the middle of an economic crisis.
items.t: Senegal: Pastef removes President Faye from its ranks

items.summary:
Former NSW opposition leader warns party against becoming ‘Labor lite’ or ‘One Nation lite’ in late-night speech

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Former New South Wales opposition leader, Mark Speakman, will not contest his seat at the March state election, the latest in a mass exodus of MPs under the Liberal leader who replaced him, Kellie Sloane.

In a late-night speech on Thursday, the final sitting day of NSW’s legislative assembly ahead of the vote, Speakman said he would not contest his south Sydney seat of Cronulla, which he has held since 2011.

items.title: Myanmar's Rohingya case: how does the ICJ define genocide?
items.summary: The ICJ is preparing to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, in a case brought by The Gambia after the 2017 crackdown. The key legal test is proving intent to destroy a group, which is notoriously hard, and the court’s reading of it could also weigh on South Africa’s case against Israel.

items.title: Guardian Australia takes home two Walkley awards for excellence in journalism
items.summary:
Stories revealing Pauline Hanson’s US trip with Gina Rinehart and the systemic betrayal of Kardell Lomas before her death recognised

Guardian Australia journalists have won two Walkley awards, one for a story about the systemic betrayal of a woman who was killed by her partner, and another for an exclusive story that revealed Pauline Hanson had travelled to the US with mining billionaire Gina Rinehart.

Investigative reporter Sarah Martin won the award for print/text news report for her exclusive story that revealed the One Nation leader and her chief of staff, James Ashby, travelled with Rinehart on the mining magnate’s Gulfstream 700 on 27 October last year.

items.title: Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked
items.summary:
The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits

Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

The baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who said they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

items.summary:
Assessment of damage under way, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia

The remaining Kerch rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was attacked overnight, leading to a halt in train services, two days after a dramatic Ukrainian air raid had knocked out the road bridge alongside.

Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.

The death of an Aboriginal woman who collapsed after drinking at least 20 litres of water in a New South Wales prison cell was preventable and the result of systemic failures, a coroner has found.

Tammy Michelle Shipley, 47, died at Silverwater women’s correctional centre on 20 December 2022.

items.title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
items.summary:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.

items.t: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns

items.title: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN
items.summary:
Almost half of women in west and central Africa cannot withhold consent, with girls worst affected, UNFPA finds

One in four women around the world have no power of consent if their husband or partner demands sex, according to a UN report.

In west and central Africa, almost half of women (45%) are not able to say no in their own marriage, while a third of women (33%) in east and southern Africa and in Arab states face the same predicament. In Latin America and the Caribbean, one in 10 women are not able to refuse sex, said the report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) published on Thursday.

Continue reading...
items.t: One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage, says UN

items.title: Florida pastor found guilty over 2021 assassination of Haitian president
items.summary:
Christian Emmanuel Sanon faces life in prison after conviction on charges arising from killing of Jovenel Moïse

A Florida pastor with dual Haitian-American citizenship was convicted on Wednesday of US charges arising from the 2021 assassination of the Haitian president Jovenel Moïse.

Christian Emmanuel Sanon was found guilty on charges including conspiring to kill Moïse after a nearly eight-week trial in federal court in Miami. He had faced a total of eight charges including conspiracy to kidnap or kill a person outside the United States.

items.title: Hegseth uses Venezuela visit to boast of Maduro’s capture by US military
items.summary:
Defense secretary asserts US dominance on trip that would have seemed ‘impossible, almost unbelievable’ a year ago

Pete Hegseth has used his first visit to Venezuela since US special forces abducted its former president, Nicolás Maduro, to boast of the dictator’s capture during what he called “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America”.

Maduro was controversially seized by Delta Force operatives in the early hours of 3 January, setting in motion an improbable rapprochement between Washington and Venezuela’s anti-imperialist “Chavista” regime, which has ruled since 1999.

items.title: Apec summit as it happened: Xi welcomes Trump on China visit as Putin claims Europe in ‘humiliating decline’
items.summary:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here

Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up?

That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday.

It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.

Continue reading...

items.title: Fears grow that US will put Nobel-winning judge under sanctions after Myanmar genocide ruling
items.summary:
A ruling against Myanmar could set precedent for court’s judgment on Israel’s actions in Gaza

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

Continue reading...
items.t: Fears grow over US sanctions on ICJ judges ahead of Myanmar genocide ruling

items.title: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt
items.summary:
Leaked documents raise questions about claims Egypt met welfare targets to qualify for €2.5bn in loans

The European Commission has been accused of sugarcoating figures to enable it to release funds to Egypt under a landmark pact with the authoritarian government of Abdel Fatah al-Sisi.

The charge relates to a €7.4bn deal promised by Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, to al-Sisi on a high-profile visit to Cairo in 2024. The three-year “strategic and comprehensive partnership” was intended to bolster Egypt’s shaky economy, deter migrants from coming to Europe and shore up a region reeling from the 7 October attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza.

Continue reading...
items.t: European Commission accused of sugarcoating figures to release funds to Egypt

items.title: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
items.summary:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams

The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.

On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.

Continue reading...
items.t: Sleeve checks and no smartglasses: South Korea races to protect all-important university exams against AI

St Kitts and Nevis to wind down citizenship-by-investment program after EU warns of end to visa-free access

The decision by St Kitts and Nevis to end a lucrative programme offering citizenship to wealthy foreigners in exchange for investment threatens its economy and ability to support people in need, the premier of the island of Nevis has warned.

On Friday, Terrance Drew, the prime minister of the twin-island Caribbean nation, announced he would wind down the citizenship-by-investment (CBI) programme, after the European Union threatened to end visa-free access for St Kitts and Nevis.

About 20 Indigenous people emerged from isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest, several organizations reported on Tuesday, raising the alarm about increased invasions into the tribe’s territory.

According to the NGO Survival International, members of the Awá people, who live in voluntary isolation, arrived on Monday in a village and made contact with a government team in a “historic encounter”.

items.title: Eight-year-old Haitian boy returns home after release from ICE custody
items.summary:
Child reunited with family after he was detained by immigration agents in San Diego and transferred to Texas

An eight-year-old Haitian boy who was put into restraints and detained by immigration agents in San Diego on 4 November and transferred to a facility in Texas has been reunited with his family in California.

Representative Juan Vargas shared a photograph of the boy and his family in a social media post on Monda, writing: “11 days ago, an 8-year-old in San Diego was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in. He was separated from his loved ones and held in a facility in Texas. Today, he’s finally home.”

Continue reading...

items.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
items.summary:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

Continue reading...
items.t: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
